title: Visuospatial Neglect: A Theory-Informed Overview of Current and Emerging Strategies and a Systematic Review on the Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is best understood not as a unitary visual deficit, but as a disorder of spatially directed attention and awareness that typically follows unilateral brain injury, most often in the right hemisphere. Clinically, patients may fail to orient, explore, or respond to contralesional stimuli despite preserved elementary sensory function, indicating a disturbance in higher-order attentional control rather than primary perception alone. This framework has been central to accounts linking neglect to large-scale attention systems that allocate salience, support orienting, and maintain spatial representations across sensory and motor domains ref [1], ref [23].

A key conceptual advance has been the shift from focal-lesion models toward network-based explanations. Neglect can arise from disruption of distributed fronto-parietal systems and their underlying white matter pathways, rather than damage to a single cortical locus. In this view, impaired spatial awareness reflects both gray-matter dysfunction within attention-related regions and disconnection between them, helping to explain the marked heterogeneity of symptoms across patients and lesion sites ref [12], ref [21].

This network perspective is especially important for therapeutic research. If neglect reflects an imbalance or breakdown within attention networks, interventions such as non-invasive brain stimulation can be rationalized as attempts to modulate dysfunctional nodes or restore interhemispheric and intrahemispheric communication. Accordingly, a theory-informed characterization of neglect begins with its status as a multidimensional syndrome rooted in distributed mechanisms of attention, orienting, and spatial representation ref [1], ref [21], ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A clinically important feature of visuospatial neglect is its heterogeneity across spatial frames and sensorimotor components. Neglect cannot be reduced to a single visual-attentional deficit; rather, patients may show abnormalities in exploratory orienting, internal updating of spatial representations, or body-centered spatial coding. In this regard, evidence that impaired spatial remapping contributes to unilateral neglect helps explain why deficits persist across eye movements and dynamic scene exploration, extending the syndrome beyond simple failure to detect contralesional stimuli ref [24].

This multidimensional view is further supported by proposals that neglect has a vestibular component. The characterization of spatial neglect as, in part, a vestibular disorder emphasizes disturbed egocentric orientation and biased estimates of body and environmental midline, thereby linking visual, postural, and oculomotor symptoms within a common spatial reference framework ref [14]. Such accounts are useful clinically because they explain why neglect may manifest not only on cancellation or line bisection tasks, but also in body-related and locomotor behavior.

Although classically associated with right-hemisphere damage, neglect is not exclusively a right-hemisphere syndrome. Acute left hemisphere stroke can also produce right hemispatial neglect, though typically with lower frequency and often different clinical prominence than the canonical left neglect after right hemisphere injury ref [34]. Longitudinal lesion evidence additionally indicates that chronic neglect is strongly predicted by damage to specific white matter pathways, underscoring that enduring symptoms reflect network-level disruption rather than isolated cortical injury ref [8]. Together, these findings reinforce the need to characterize neglect in terms of distributed systems, multiple spatial operations, and variable clinical phenotypes.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A clinically important feature of visuospatial neglect is that it rarely reflects a unitary left–right perceptual loss. Rather, neglect often co-occurs with deficits in arousal, orienting, exploratory behavior, and multisensory body-space representations, which helps explain its marked heterogeneity across patients. A broad neuropsychological framing therefore distinguishes neglect from related spatial syndromes while emphasizing that its manifestations can involve personal, peripersonal, and extrapersonal space, as well as perceptual and representational domains ref [33].

This multidimensionality is reinforced by evidence that nonspatial factors such as tonic and phasic alertness can modulate spatial bias. Reduced alertness may exacerbate ipsilesional orienting tendencies and worsen performance on cancellation or visual search tasks, indicating that neglect severity is partly shaped by general attentional state rather than spatial coding alone ref [16]. Such findings are theoretically relevant because they complicate purely lateralized accounts and support models in which spatial and nonspatial attention interact dynamically in the expression of neglect.

Anatomically, this broader view is consistent with lesion evidence showing that neglect may arise not only from focal cortical damage but also from disconnection of fronto-parietal and temporo-parietal white-matter pathways. DTI tractography studies have linked neglect to disruption of long-range association fibers, underscoring that impaired spatial awareness can emerge from network-level breakdown rather than a single cortical epicenter ref [8]. In parallel, vestibular contributions are increasingly recognized: vestibular processing influences spatial orientation, egocentric reference frames, and body-centered representations, providing an important route through which bodily and environmental space are integrated ref [26]. Together, these observations position neglect as a disorder of distributed spatial cognition with strong implications for theory-driven rehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A clinically important aspect of visuospatial neglect is its frequent co-occurrence with related disturbances such as extinction and anosognosia, which together shape both syndrome expression and functional burden. Acute-stage work indicates that neglect and extinction should not be treated as interchangeable signs: although they often overlap after right-hemisphere stroke, they can reflect partially distinct dysfunctional states within the visuospatial attention system, with extinction emerging most clearly under competitive stimulation conditions and neglect affecting more basic orienting and exploratory behavior ref [15]. This distinction is relevant for clinical characterization because bedside performance may vary substantially depending on task demands and sensory competition.

The anatomical heterogeneity of these deficits further supports a network-based account rather than a single-lesion model. Reviews of functional neuroanatomy emphasize that spatial neglect is linked to distributed parietal, frontal, and temporo-parietal systems and to their interactions, while also noting the persistent challenge of mapping specific symptoms onto circumscribed cortical territories ref [19]. Consistent with this view, perfusion-based imaging in patients with basal ganglia lesions has shown that neglect may arise not only from focal subcortical injury itself but also from remote cortical dysfunction within common attention-related regions, highlighting diaschisis and network disruption as key mechanisms ref [16].

From a clinical standpoint, these associated syndromes are not merely descriptive epiphenomena. In right-hemispheric stroke, neglect, extinction, anosognosia, and lesion site each contribute to reduced independence in activities of daily living, underscoring that careful phenotyping has direct prognostic significance ref [15]. Altogether, the dissociation between neglect and extinction, the contribution of subcortical-cortical network dysfunction, and the impact of co-occurring unawareness reinforce the need for multidimensional assessment when interpreting treatment effects and selecting candidates for neuromodulatory interventions ref [15], ref [16], ref [15], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
At a theoretical level, visuospatial neglect is significant because it exposes how spatial cognition depends on asymmetric but interactive hemispheric contributions. Early accounts of global orientation emphasized a dominant role of the right hemisphere in constructing organism-centered spatial frameworks, helping to explain why right-hemisphere lesions more often produce severe and persistent contralesional neglect than comparable left-hemisphere damage ref [25]. This asymmetry is not simply sensory or motor; rather, neglect reflects a disturbance in the allocation of spatial priority across internal representations of extrapersonal space.

Contemporary models further suggest that neglect is a network disorder in which large-scale coordination of attentional systems is disrupted. Oscillatory synchrony has been proposed as a core mechanism by which distributed cortical regions transiently bind relevant information and bias selection toward behaviorally salient stimuli ref [30]. In this framework, neglect can be understood as a pathological imbalance in interregional communication, particularly affecting the dynamic coupling required to orient, maintain, and reorient attention toward the contralesional side ref [30].

These conceptual perspectives are especially relevant for treatment development. If neglect arises from hemispheric asymmetry combined with impaired network-level synchronization, then interventions need not be limited to compensatory training alone; they may also aim to rebalance activity between hemispheres or restore more adaptive temporal coordination within attention networks ref [25], ref [30]. This logic provides an important theoretical bridge to non-invasive brain stimulation, whose rationale often rests on modulating precisely these abnormal patterns of lateralization and network interaction.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A foundational model for neglect rehabilitation conceptualizes the syndrome as a disorder of large-scale attention networks rather than a unitary sensory deficit. In this view, neglect emerges when right-lateralized systems supporting spatial orienting and nonspatial alerting are disrupted, with consequent failures to allocate attention toward contralesional space and to reconfigure behavior in response to salient events ref [1], ref [23]. This network account helps explain the heterogeneity of neglect and motivates treatments aimed at restoring attentional orienting, increasing tonic/phasic alertness, or recruiting preserved network components.

A complementary formulation emphasizes neglect as a disconnection syndrome. Beyond focal cortical injury, behavioral impairment can follow damage to white-matter pathways linking parietal, frontal, and temporal regions that collectively support spatial awareness ref [12], ref [21]. From a rehabilitation perspective, this predicts that recovery may depend not only on local lesion site but also on the integrity of residual network connectivity. Accordingly, interventions are often designed to strengthen communication within surviving circuits, compensate for impaired fronto-parietal coordination, or leverage alternative pathways for attentional control ref [12], ref [21].

These models also support the influential interhemispheric-competition account, according to which unilateral damage produces an imbalance in reciprocal attentional control between the hemispheres. Evidence from transient perturbation studies shows that inducing a 'virtual lesion' in parietal cortex can bias spatial attention ipsilaterally, mirroring core features of neglect and suggesting a causal role for abnormal hemispheric weighting ref [7]. This framework directly informs non-invasive brain stimulation strategies: inhibitory stimulation of the intact hemisphere or excitatory stimulation of the lesioned hemisphere is hypothesized to rebalance network dynamics and reduce pathological orienting biases ref [7], ref [1], ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A complementary theoretical account treats neglect not only as a deficit of static spatial representation, but as a disorder of dynamic spatial updating and body-centered orientation. On this view, patients may fail to remap contralesional events across eye, head, or trunk movements, so that spatial information is not reliably updated into current coordinates. Such remapping deficits can help explain why neglect persists in visually explored environments and why some patients show marked difficulty when targets must be tracked across successive positions or shifts in gaze ref [24].

This perspective also aligns with vestibular models, which emphasize disturbed internal estimates of egocentric orientation and straight-ahead. The proposal that neglect has a vestibular component broadens the syndrome beyond visual-attentional bias, suggesting that abnormal spatial anchoring of the body in space may contribute to ipsilesional deviation in exploration and awareness ref [14]. Clinical observations that neglect-like symptoms can also follow acute left hemisphere lesions, albeit typically less often and with different phenomenology, further caution against overly simple right-hemisphere accounts and support models centered on disrupted coordinate transformations and spatial reference frames ref [34].

For rehabilitation, these models motivate interventions designed to recalibrate egocentric coordinates rather than merely increase leftward search. Vestibular stimulation and other sensory manipulations can be interpreted as attempts to reset distorted spatial reference frames, while therapies that require active exploration across movements may train spatial updating mechanisms ref [14], ref [24]. Longitudinal lesion evidence additionally suggests that chronic neglect is strongly shaped by white-matter damage, indicating that successful recovery depends on restoring communication within distributed networks that support remapping and spatial orientation, not solely on compensating for a focal cortical lesion ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A third influential framework conceptualizes neglect not only as a lateralized orienting disorder, but as a disturbance of distributed state regulation and multisensory spatial calibration. Clinical overviews emphasize that neglect symptoms fluctuate with task demands and often co-occur with broader impairments in spatial representation, bodily orientation, and exploratory behavior, suggesting that rehabilitation must address both spatially specific and domain-general components of attention ref [33]. In particular, reduced tonic and phasic alertness can exacerbate contralesional omissions, supporting models in which nonspatial vigilance mechanisms interact with spatial bias rather than operating independently ref [16].

This perspective also helps explain the therapeutic rationale for vestibular and other sensory stimulation approaches. The vestibular system contributes to egocentric orientation, body-centered reference frames, and higher-order spatial cognition, making it a plausible entry point for transiently recalibrating distorted spatial maps in neglect ref [26]. Likewise, tractography studies indicate that neglect frequently reflects disconnection across fronto-parietal and temporo-parietal white-matter pathways rather than damage to a single cortical locus, reinforcing the idea that impaired integration across attention, arousal, and sensorimotor networks is central to the syndrome ref [8].

For neuromodulation, this model predicts that effective stimulation should modify network state and interregional communication, not merely excite a focal cortical area. Work on transcranial magnetic stimulation highlights that perceptual effects arise through changes in ongoing neural activity and context-dependent network interactions ref [27]. By contrast, the observation that high-gamma tACS over early visual cortex can improve contrast perception without altering spatial attention underscores that boosting low-level sensory gain alone may be insufficient for neglect, unless stimulation engages the broader attentional architecture implicated by these state-based models ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A further influential framework conceptualizes neglect as a disorder of distributed spatial-attention networks rather than a unitary visuoperceptual deficit. Neuroanatomical mapping studies emphasize that neglect can arise from damage to partially distinct cortical and subcortical nodes, particularly within parietal systems and their wider functional connections, helping explain the marked heterogeneity of clinical presentations ref [19]. This view is reinforced by evidence that acute neglect and extinction may reflect different functional states of the visuospatial attention system, implying that rehabilitation should be tailored to the dominant deficit profile rather than applied as a generic treatment package ref [22].

Subcortical evidence also supports a network model with important therapeutic implications. In patients with basal ganglia lesions, perfusion imaging has identified common cortical dysfunction remote from the structural lesion, consistent with diaschisis and secondary disruption of attention networks ref [15]. Such findings justify interventions aimed at re-engaging dysfunctional but structurally intact cortex, including neuromodulation approaches designed to normalize activity in distributed frontoparietal circuits rather than focusing only on the lesion core ref [15], ref [19].

This network account also intersects with multimodal and functional rehabilitation perspectives. Experimental work on multisensory experience shows that cross-modal inputs can shape subsequent unisensory processing, providing a theoretical basis for therapies that use audiovisual, somatosensory, or sensorimotor cueing to recalibrate spatial representations ref [11]. Clinically, the close association of neglect, extinction, anosognosia, and lesion site with disability in activities of daily living underscores that rehabilitation must address interacting attentional and awareness deficits if gains are to generalize beyond laboratory tasks ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A complementary theoretical strand frames neglect as a disorder of multisensory spatial binding and predictive coordination rather than a purely visual-attentional deficit. On this view, spatial awareness depends on the brain’s ability to align information across modalities and over time, so that visual, auditory, proprioceptive, and vestibular signals converge into a coherent estimate of egocentric space. Work on audiovisual synchrony and crossmodal prediction supports the idea that temporal coincidence and learned expectations are central to perceptual selection, with direct relevance for explaining why neglected stimuli may fail to gain access to awareness when cross-sensory integration is degraded or asymmetrically weighted ref [17], ref [27].

This framework helps explain why rehabilitation strategies that combine visual scanning with auditory cueing, prism adaptation with proprioceptive feedback, or vestibular stimulation with visual tasks can sometimes outperform strictly unimodal approaches. It also broadens the rationale for interventions targeting internal spatial models: electrophysiological evidence on mental imagery and embodied simulation suggests that spatial representations are not restricted to online sensory input but are supported by distributed simulation processes, which may be exploitable in imagery-based or action-oriented training ref [21]. In parallel, theories of global spatial orientation and hemispheric lateralization imply that neglect may reflect a disturbed reference frame for whole-body orientation in space, not only a lateralized defect in stimulus detection ref [25].

For non-invasive brain stimulation, these models motivate attempts to restore coordinated network dynamics rather than only to increase or suppress activity in a single cortical node. Oscillatory synchrony has been proposed as a core mechanism of attentional selection, making rhythmic stimulation and connectivity-oriented protocols conceptually attractive when neglect is understood as a disorder of large-scale temporal coupling ref [30]. More generally, a multisensory-predictive account encourages treatment designs that pair brain stimulation with concurrent crossmodal tasks, with the aim of recalibrating spatial priors, temporal binding, and embodied representations together ref [17], ref [27], ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A useful point of departure for non-stimulation rehabilitation is the network account of visuospatial neglect. Rather than reflecting a unitary sensory deficit, neglect is now understood as a disorder of large-scale attention systems, especially interactions between dorsal and ventral fronto-parietal networks that support orienting, target selection, and reorienting to salient events ref [1], ref [23]. This framework helps explain why patients show heterogeneous impairments across exploratory behavior, sustained attention, and spatial awareness, and why effective rehabilitation often combines compensatory and restorative elements rather than targeting a single symptom.

Lesion evidence further indicates that neglect frequently arises from disconnection within these attention systems. Classic accounts describe left neglect after right-hemisphere stroke as a disconnection syndrome in which damage to long-range pathways disrupts coordinated processing across parietal, frontal, and temporal regions ref [12]. More recent structural-functional syntheses reinforce this view, showing that both white-matter injury and dysfunction of distributed gray-matter nodes contribute to impaired spatial awareness ref [21]. For rehabilitation, this implies that behavioral interventions should be designed not only to shift gaze or scanning direction, but also to recruit intact network components and promote more efficient interregional coordination.

Accordingly, established non-stimulation approaches such as visual scanning training, cueing procedures, and task-specific exploration therapies can be interpreted as attempts to externally scaffold deficient attentional control. Their clinical rationale is strongest when grounded in theory: interventions that increase phasic alerting, enhance reorienting to contralesional space, or structure exploratory routines are broadly consistent with contemporary models of attention and neglect ref [1], ref [23]. This theory-informed perspective is also important for evaluating emerging treatments, because it frames behavioral rehabilitation as network compensation and reweighting rather than simple perceptual retraining ref [12], ref [21].

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A second important cluster of non-stimulation interventions targets bodily and spatial reference frames, particularly through vestibular and sensorimotor mechanisms. The rationale is that neglect is not solely a visual-attentional disorder: altered egocentric coding, disturbed body-centered orientation, and impaired updating of spatial representations can all contribute to the syndrome. This broader view is consistent with proposals that some forms of neglect reflect dysfunction in vestibularly mediated spatial orientation and with evidence that deficits in spatial remapping are a core component in at least a subset of patients ref [14], ref [24].

Clinically, this framework has motivated interventions such as caloric or galvanic vestibular stimulation, neck-muscle vibration, trunk rotation, and other techniques designed to transiently rebalance spatial coordinates without directly stimulating cortex. Their appeal lies in the possibility of rapidly shifting exploratory behavior and improving awareness of contralesional space, although effects are often short-lived and may vary depending on the integrity of the underlying network. Longitudinal lesion work suggests that chronic persistence of neglect is strongly shaped by white-matter damage, implying that response to these approaches may depend on whether core fronto-parietal communication pathways remain sufficiently preserved to support recalibration ref [8].

This perspective also has implications for patient selection. Neglect is most classically associated with right-hemisphere injury, yet clinically meaningful hemispatial neglect can also follow acute left-hemisphere stroke, reminding clinicians that rehabilitation should be guided by symptom profile rather than lesion side alone ref [34]. Overall, body- and vestibular-oriented therapies are best viewed as mechanistically informative, low-cost adjuncts that may be especially useful when combined with sustained training aimed at consolidating transient gains in spatial orienting and remapping ref [14], ref [24], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A distinct cluster of non-stimulation approaches targets nonvisual state variables that modulate neglect, particularly alertness and vestibular-somatosensory signals. This rationale is theory-informed: neglect is not solely a spatial representational deficit, but often reflects impaired deployment of attention across interacting arousal, orienting, and multisensory systems. Experimental evidence that tonic and phasic alertness influence both spatial and nonspatial aspects of visual attention provides a basis for behavioral interventions that increase readiness to respond, for example through warning cues or sustained-attention training ref [16]. Broader clinical syntheses similarly emphasize that neglect is heterogeneous and frequently co-occurs with deficits in exploratory behavior and body-centered spatial processing, supporting multimodal rehabilitation strategies rather than purely visuomotor retraining ref [33].

Within this framework, vestibular-based interventions remain of particular interest. The vestibular system contributes not only to balance, but also to egocentric spatial coding, bodily orientation, and higher-order attentional functions, making it a plausible leverage point for transiently rebalancing spatial behavior in neglect ref [26]. Caloric, galvanic, or motion-related vestibular manipulations have therefore been explored as adjunctive techniques to bias attention toward contralesional space, although their clinical effects are often short-lived and their practical deployment can be limited by tolerability and logistical constraints ref [26], ref [33].

Patient stratification is likely crucial for these approaches. Tractography studies show that neglect is associated with variable white-matter damage affecting fronto-parietal and temporo-parietal connections, implying that response to alertness-based or vestibular interventions may depend on the integrity of large-scale networks rather than lesion location alone ref [8]. Accordingly, current practice increasingly views these methods as useful components of individualized, combined rehabilitation programs—especially when the aim is to transiently enhance exploration or engagement—rather than as stand-alone restorative treatments ref [8], ref [16], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A further class of non-stimulation interventions targets reduced awareness of deficit and impaired transfer to everyday function. This rationale is clinically important because neglect rarely occurs in isolation: anosognosia and extinction frequently co-occur, and their combined presence is associated with substantially poorer activities of daily living after right-hemisphere stroke, beyond lesion site alone ref [15]. Rehabilitation strategies in this domain therefore emphasize explicit feedback, guided error detection, cueing during functional tasks, and repeated practice in ecologically meaningful contexts rather than relying only on paper-and-pencil improvement.

The theoretical basis for such approaches is supported by work showing that acute neglect and extinction reflect partially distinct functional states within the visuospatial attention system ref [16]. This distinction matters therapeutically: patients whose performance is dominated by stimulus competition or extinction may benefit from graded task structuring and reduced visual crowding, whereas those with broader neglect may require more intensive compensatory scanning and sustained supervision during daily activities ref [16]. In parallel, lesion-symptom mapping indicates that neglect arises from damage to distributed parietal and extra-parietal networks rather than a single cortical module, reinforcing the need for multimodal, individualized rehabilitation programs that address attention, awareness, and task context together ref [19].

Clinically, these observations support function-oriented treatment models in which neglect therapy is embedded within dressing, mobility, wheelchair navigation, eating, and reading practice, with explicit monitoring for poor insight and extinction-related failures ref [15], ref [19]. Although such approaches are less mechanistically circumscribed than prism adaptation or sensory manipulations, they are highly applicable in routine stroke rehabilitation because they directly target disability and safety. In this respect, theory-informed functional rehabilitation provides an essential comparator and complement to emerging neuromodulatory approaches ref [16], ref [15], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A further emerging direction is to target higher-order spatial orientation and temporal coordination mechanisms rather than only sensory input or overt scanning behavior. Neglect has long been linked to hemispheric asymmetries in global orientation in space, with right-hemisphere systems contributing disproportionately to the construction of broad spatial reference frames; this provides a rationale for interventions designed to recalibrate egocentric orientation, body-centered spatial coding, or whole-field attentional anchoring rather than merely training detection of left-sided targets ref [25].

In parallel, network-level accounts of attention emphasize that effective orienting depends on coordinated oscillatory interactions across distributed cortical systems. From this perspective, behavioral and multisensory therapies may be viewed as attempts to restore temporal coupling within damaged attention networks by increasing salience, prediction, and crossmodal coherence, thereby improving selection of contralesional events ref [30]. Evidence from studies of multisensory experience and audiovisual synchrony supports the broader principle that temporally aligned inputs can reshape subsequent perceptual processing and attentional allocation, suggesting a mechanistic basis for structured crossmodal cueing paradigms in neglect rehabilitation ref [21], ref [22], ref [23].

Clinically, these approaches remain heterogeneous and more theory-driven than standardized, but they are attractive because they are low risk and can be embedded into task-oriented therapy. Their main promise is not that they replace established compensatory methods, but that they may strengthen spatial orienting by acting on supramodal reference frames and large-scale attentional coordination. This conceptual bridge is especially important when situating non-invasive brain stimulation within the wider rehabilitation landscape, since stimulation-based protocols often aim to modulate the same lateralized and network-dynamic mechanisms identified by these non-stimulation approaches ref [25], ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A mechanistic starting point for non-invasive brain stimulation in visuospatial neglect is the network view of spatial attention. Neglect is not reducible to a single cortical epicenter, but reflects dysfunction within distributed dorsal and ventral attention systems, together with disturbed interactions between hemispheres that bias orienting toward the ipsilesional side ref [1], ref [23]. This framing is central for therapeutic stimulation because it implies that clinical benefit may arise either from downregulating maladaptively dominant contralesional regions or from facilitating residual activity within damaged right-hemisphere attention circuits.

The rationale for these approaches is strengthened by lesion models that describe neglect as a disconnection syndrome rather than a purely focal cortical deficit. Structural interruption of fronto-parietal and temporo-parietal pathways can degrade spatial awareness even when classical cortical nodes are only partially damaged, and combined gray-matter dysfunction with white-matter disconnection helps explain the heterogeneity of neglect phenotypes ref [12], ref [21]. Accordingly, stimulation targets are best conceived as entry points into larger attention networks, with expected effects depending on whether stimulation restores intrahemispheric processing, rebalances interhemispheric competition, or modulates network-level compensation.

Evidence from healthy-participant TMS studies provided an important proof of principle for this therapeutic logic. Inducing transient 'virtual lesions' in parietal cortex can shift spatial attention and even enhance ipsilateral attentional performance, demonstrating that altering parietal excitability is sufficient to rebalance attentional allocation ref [7]. In rehabilitation, this experimental observation supports the use of inhibitory stimulation over the intact left posterior parietal cortex or facilitatory stimulation over damaged right-hemisphere regions, with protocol design guided by the specific network abnormality inferred in each patient ref [1], ref [21].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A theory-informed account of non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) in neglect must begin from the heterogeneity of the syndrome. Neglect is not reducible to a unitary visual-attentional deficit: left-hemisphere lesions can also produce right hemispatial neglect, although less frequently, underscoring the bilateral and network-dependent character of spatial orienting deficits ref [34]. Likewise, longitudinal lesion evidence indicates that chronic neglect severity is shaped by white-matter damage patterns, suggesting that stimulation effects will depend not only on cortical target choice but also on the integrity of structural pathways capable of propagating induced activity changes ref [8].

These observations have direct mechanistic implications for protocol design. If neglect partly reflects impaired spatial remapping, then stimulation over parietal or parieto-frontal nodes may be expected to influence updating of spatial representations rather than merely boost detection performance ref [24]. In parallel, vestibular accounts of neglect imply that some NIBS interventions may act by recalibrating egocentric reference frames or multisensory spatial alignment, especially when paired with behavioral tasks engaging body-centered orientation ref [14]. Such frameworks argue against a one-size-fits-all approach and instead favor matching the stimulation site and behavioral context to the dominant deficit profile.

Accordingly, contemporary therapeutic protocols should be interpreted as attempts to modulate distributed spatial computations within a damaged network. Patients with extensive disconnection may show weaker or less durable responses, whereas those with relatively preserved pathways may better translate transient physiological modulation into functional gains ref [8]. The same logic also supports combining NIBS with remapping-intensive or vestibularly enriched rehabilitation paradigms, because mechanistic congruence between stimulation target and task demands is likely to be a major determinant of efficacy ref [24], ref [14], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central issue in protocol design is the choice of mechanistic target. In visuospatial neglect, non-invasive brain stimulation is not simply used to increase or decrease excitability locally; rather, it aims to rebalance distributed attention systems whose disruption may reflect both cortical dysfunction and white-matter disconnection. Tractography work in stroke neglect underscores that behavioral deficits often arise from damage to fronto-parietal pathways rather than a single node, implying that stimulation effects depend on residual network integrity and the capacity of connected regions to support compensatory reorganization ref [8]. This network view is consistent with broader clinical descriptions of neglect as a heterogeneous spatial disorder with multiple component deficits that may respond differently to stimulation timing and site selection ref [33].

At the modality level, TMS and transcranial electrical stimulation engage partly distinct neurophysiological mechanisms. TMS can transiently perturb or facilitate neural processing depending on pulse pattern, state dependency, and the excitability of the stimulated cortex, making it well suited for probing causal contributions of parietal and frontal regions to spatial awareness ref [27]. By contrast, alternating-current approaches are often motivated by the hypothesis that attentional deficits involve abnormal oscillatory coordination; however, available evidence also cautions against assuming straightforward behavioral transfer from sensory enhancement to attentional remediation, since high-gamma tACS over visual cortex can improve contrast perception without modulating spatial attention ref [31].

Protocol efficacy is also shaped by non-spatial modulators. Alertness strongly interacts with spatial performance, suggesting that stimulation delivered when tonic or phasic arousal is optimized may yield larger gains than anatomically identical stimulation delivered in a low-alertness state ref [16]. Likewise, vestibular contributions to spatial cognition provide a rationale for combining brain stimulation with multisensory or vestibular-oriented rehabilitation, particularly when the therapeutic goal is to influence body-centered and world-centered reference frames rather than visual exploration alone ref [26]. Together, these considerations argue for mechanism-informed, individualized protocols that integrate lesion anatomy, target network physiology, and the patient’s current cognitive state ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central issue in protocol design for non-invasive brain stimulation in neglect is target selection based on the distributed, state-dependent anatomy of the syndrome. Functional-anatomical accounts show that neglect is not reducible to a single cortical locus, but reflects dysfunction across parietal and connected attention networks, with substantial inter-individual variability in lesion topography and residual network integrity ref [19]. This has direct therapeutic implications: stimulation sites and expected effects should be chosen in relation to the dominant behavioral phenotype, rather than by adopting a uniform parietal montage for all patients.

The need for individualized targeting is reinforced by evidence that structurally different lesions may converge on common dysfunctional territories. In patients with basal ganglia neglect, perfusion imaging identified cortical regions of hypofunction despite subcortical damage, suggesting that stimulation may need to engage downstream cortical nodes rather than only the visible lesion site ref [16]. Likewise, acute neglect and extinction can reflect partially distinct functional states within the visuospatial attention system, implying that inhibitory or facilitatory protocols may differentially benefit patients depending on whether their presentation is dominated by spatial bias, competitive extinction, or both ref [15].

Clinical protocol design should therefore integrate mechanistic and pragmatic considerations. Because neglect severity, extinction, anosognosia, and lesion site all influence functional disability, stimulation studies should stratify patients on these dimensions and align outcome measures with everyday behavior rather than relying exclusively on paper-and-pencil tests ref [15]. More broadly, the continuing challenge in the field is to translate complex lesion-network models of parietal function into reproducible stimulation strategies, balancing anatomical precision with feasibility in routine rehabilitation settings ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final design consideration concerns how stimulation protocols are aligned with the temporal dynamics of attention networks. Neglect is not only a disorder of focal cortical damage, but also of altered hemispheric balance and disrupted large-scale coordination of spatial representations, with a marked right-hemisphere specialization for global orienting in space ref [25]. This framework supports protocol choices that aim either to downregulate maladaptive hyperexcitability in the contralesional hemisphere or to restore more symmetric interhemispheric engagement, depending on lesion site, chronicity, and behavioral phenotype.

From a mechanistic perspective, these decisions are increasingly informed by network-level models of attention in which effective selection depends on oscillatory coordination across distributed cortical populations ref [30]. In this view, non-invasive brain stimulation may act not simply by changing local excitability, but by biasing phase relationships, synchrony, and communication efficiency within fronto-parietal systems ref [30]. Such considerations are especially relevant when comparing repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, transcranial direct current stimulation, and frequency-specific alternating-current approaches, because their therapeutic effects may differ according to whether the intended target is tonic excitability, interhemispheric competition, or rhythmic coupling.

Accordingly, protocol design in neglect rehabilitation should be interpreted as a problem of matching stimulation modality, site, polarity or frequency, and treatment schedule to the patient’s underlying network disturbance. Theory-driven personalization remains important: patients with predominant directional orienting deficits may benefit most from interventions grounded in hemispheric lateralization models ref [25], whereas patients with more diffuse attentional instability may require approaches that better engage distributed oscillatory mechanisms ref [30]. This mechanistic framing helps explain the heterogeneity of clinical outcomes and provides a rationale for combining brain stimulation with behavioral training that recruits the same spatial-attentional circuits.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A systematic review of non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) for visuospatial neglect must begin from the pathophysiological rationale that has most strongly guided intervention design: neglect is not reducible to a focal cortical deficit, but reflects disruption of large-scale attention networks and their interhemispheric balance. Network accounts emphasize asymmetric interactions between dorsal and ventral attention systems after right-hemisphere damage, providing the theoretical basis for inhibitory stimulation of the intact hemisphere or facilitatory stimulation of lesioned-network nodes ref [1], ref [23].

This rationale is further supported by disconnection models showing that neglect severity depends not only on cortical lesion site but also on interruption of fronto-parietal and parieto-temporal white-matter pathways. Accordingly, the clinical heterogeneity seen across NIBS studies is plausibly linked to variation in structural disconnection, residual network integrity, and lesion topography rather than stimulation protocol alone ref [12], ref [21]. These considerations are essential when interpreting mixed therapeutic findings, because patients grouped under the label of neglect may differ substantially in the neural substrate available for modulation.

Experimental brain-stimulation work in healthy participants also contributed directly to the clinical logic of NIBS in neglect. Reversible disruption of parietal cortex with rTMS can induce attention shifts resembling pathological spatial bias, demonstrating a causal role of parietal interhemispheric competition in orienting behavior ref [7]. In the systematic review context, this mechanistic background helps explain why most therapeutic trials have targeted parietal regions and why comparative efficacy cannot be judged solely by nominal modality (rTMS versus tDCS), but must be interpreted against the underlying network model, lesion-disconnection profile, and intended direction of hemispheric rebalancing ref [1], ref [21].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A recurrent source of heterogeneity in the clinical non-invasive brain stimulation literature is that visuospatial neglect is not a unitary syndrome. Longitudinal lesion evidence indicates that chronic neglect severity is shaped not only by cortical injury but also by white-matter disconnection, implying that stimulation response may depend on residual network integrity rather than lesion side or volume alone ref [8]. This is clinically important because trials often aggregate patients with different structural substrates, while neglect symptoms may also emerge after left hemisphere stroke, albeit less frequently and with distinct phenomenology, further complicating cohort comparability ref [34].

Behavioral-neurocognitive accounts likewise suggest that treatment effects should not be interpreted as simple shifts of spatial bias. Spatial remapping deficits have been proposed as one mechanism contributing to neglect, indicating that impaired updating across eye- and body-centered reference frames may limit the generalization of stimulation-induced gains from cancellation tasks to more ecological behaviors ref [24]. In parallel, vestibular models emphasize that neglect can involve disrupted multisensory representations of body and space, providing a rationale for why stimulation protocols combined with sensorimotor or vestibular-oriented rehabilitation may outperform stimulation delivered in isolation ref [14].

Within a systematic review framework, these observations argue for stratifying evidence by lesion topology, chronicity, and dominant neglect component rather than by stimulation modality alone. Apparent inconsistencies across rTMS or tDCS studies may therefore reflect differences in underlying disconnection patterns, remapping impairment, or vestibular-spatial dysfunction, as well as the inclusion of uncommon left-hemisphere cases with non-equivalent profiles ref [8], ref [24], ref [14], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A recurrent finding across the reviewed non-invasive brain stimulation studies is that treatment response in visuospatial neglect depends strongly on the functional architecture being targeted rather than on stimulation parameters alone. Classical clinical descriptions already emphasize that neglect is a heterogeneous syndrome spanning perceptual, representational, and exploratory deficits, making pooled efficacy estimates difficult to interpret when trials use broad inclusion criteria without phenotypic stratification ref [33]. This heterogeneity is further compounded by variation in lesion topology, particularly the degree of fronto-parietal and inter-regional disconnection visible on tractography, which is likely to influence whether stimulation can effectively engage residual attention networks ref [8].

Mechanistically, the stimulation literature also suggests that behavioral gains may arise through partially distinct routes. TMS can alter perceptual processing by changing cortical excitability and network interactions, but these effects are state-dependent and may differ across damaged versus intact hemispheric systems ref [27]. Likewise, attentional performance in neglect is not reducible to spatial bias alone: tonic and phasic alertness substantially shape both spatial and nonspatial components of visual attention, implying that trials failing to monitor arousal may misattribute improvement or nonresponse to the stimulation protocol itself ref [16]. This consideration is especially relevant when outcome batteries mix cancellation, line bisection, and reaction-time tasks that place different demands on sustained alertness.

The review also indicates that some emerging stimulation approaches remain mechanistically interesting but clinically underdetermined. For example, oscillatory entrainment paradigms cannot be assumed to generalize to neglect simply because they modulate early visual performance in healthy observers; high-gamma tACS over V1 improves contrast perception without reliably shifting spatial attention, underscoring a gap between sensory enhancement and neglect rehabilitation targets ref [31]. Relatedly, vestibular contributions to spatial orientation and body-centered coding provide a plausible rationale for multisystem neuromodulation strategies, but they also highlight why stimulation effects may differ according to whether a patient's deficit is primarily visuospatial, postural, or multimodal ref [26]. Overall, inconsistency in the clinical evidence is best understood as the product of syndrome heterogeneity, network disconnection, and task-dependent treatment mechanisms rather than simple variation in dose alone ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A recurrent source of heterogeneity in the non-invasive brain stimulation literature is the marked clinical and anatomical variability of visuospatial neglect itself. Work dissociating neglect from extinction indicates that these syndromes can reflect partially distinct functional states of the visuospatial attention system rather than a single unitary disorder, implying that patients enrolled under the same diagnostic label may differ substantially in the mechanisms available for modulation by stimulation ref [15]. This problem is compounded by the broad and still debated neuroanatomical architecture of neglect, which spans parietal, frontal, subcortical, and network-level dysfunctions ref [19].

From a systematic review perspective, this variability limits direct comparison of stimulation protocols across studies. Subcortical cases, for example, may express neglect through remote cortical dysfunction, as shown by perfusion-based evidence in patients with basal ganglia lesions, suggesting that apparent lesion location does not necessarily identify the true physiological target for intervention ref [16]. Such findings are highly relevant for NIBS trials, because stimulation site selection based solely on structural lesion topography may mismatch the distributed network disturbance actually sustaining neglect ref [16], ref [19].

Clinical outcome interpretation is further complicated by the imperfect relationship between paper-and-pencil neglect measures and real-world disability. Neglect, extinction, anosognosia, and lesion site each contribute to activities-of-daily-living impairment after right hemisphere stroke, indicating that therapeutic efficacy should not be inferred from a single cancellation or line-bisection endpoint alone ref [15]. Accordingly, inconsistent results across NIBS studies likely reflect not only differences in stimulation parameters, but also variation in neglect subtype, diaschisis patterns, and the functional outcomes selected to define response ref [15], ref [15], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A recurrent source of heterogeneity across non-invasive brain stimulation studies in visuospatial neglect is the mismatch between broad theoretical models of spatial asymmetry and the narrow operationalization of treatment outcomes. Clinical trials typically quantify change with cancellation, line bisection, or reading tasks, yet neglect reflects a wider disturbance of global spatial orientation and hemispheric specialization, not a unitary visual deficit. This theoretical point is important when interpreting apparently discordant stimulation effects across protocols and patient groups, because improvement on one task may index only partial rebalancing of spatial representations rather than generalized functional recovery ref [25].

Within a systematic review framework, this implies that between-study inconsistency should not be attributed solely to stimulation parameters. Variation in lesion topology, stage after stroke, baseline severity, and the specific reference frame probed by outcome measures can all modulate whether a given intervention appears effective. Studies that do not distinguish perceptual-attentional from exploratory-motor components, or personal from extrapersonal neglect, are especially difficult to compare, since stimulation may preferentially influence one component of spatial orientation while leaving others relatively unchanged ref [25].

Accordingly, the current clinical evidence base is best read as supporting a conditional rather than uniform therapeutic signal for non-invasive brain stimulation in neglect. Future trials should align target selection and endpoint choice with explicit models of hemispheric lateralization and large-scale spatial orientation, combine standardized core measures with ecologically relevant functional outcomes, and stratify patients by neglect subtype. Such theory-informed harmonization would substantially improve cross-trial comparability and clarify whether neuromodulation yields durable benefits beyond task-specific gains ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central translational priority is to move from syndrome-level treatment selection to mechanism-based stratification. Contemporary models frame visuospatial neglect as a disorder of large-scale attention systems rather than a unitary spatial deficit, implicating interactions between dorsal and ventral attention networks and their hemispheric balance ref [1], ref [23]. This perspective argues for patient profiling that distinguishes, for example, predominant network imbalance, impaired disengagement, or broader non-spatial attentional control deficits, because each mechanism may predict differential responsiveness to rehabilitation and non-invasive brain stimulation.

Precision neurorehabilitation will also require biomarkers that capture both structural disconnection and dynamic physiological state. Neglect has been repeatedly conceptualized as a disconnection syndrome, with white-matter damage and distributed gray-matter dysfunction jointly constraining recovery potential and targetability ref [12], ref [21]. At the same time, oscillatory markers may offer state-sensitive indicators of residual inhibitory control and attentional selection: alpha-band activity has been linked to successful suppression of unattended input, suggesting a plausible physiological readout for monitoring treatment engagement or tailoring stimulation timing ref [10]. Combining connectomic and electrophysiological markers could therefore support a more rational matching of patients to specific neuromodulatory or behavioral interventions.

A further implication is that stimulation protocols should be developed as experimental probes of individual network pathology, not only as generic therapeutic add-ons. Evidence from parietal rTMS 'virtual lesion' studies demonstrates that perturbing one node can shift spatial attention and alter interhemispheric competition ref [7], providing a mechanistic template for adaptive, model-driven intervention design. In future trials, this logic could be extended by using baseline network and oscillatory biomarkers to determine whether a patient is more likely to benefit from inhibitory, excitatory, or combined multimodal approaches, thereby improving both efficacy and interpretability of neglect rehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central translational priority is to move from anatomically broad neglect categories toward mechanism-based patient stratification. Longitudinal evidence that specific white-matter lesions predict chronic neglect supports the use of structural disconnection markers to identify patients at risk for persistent deficits and to guide treatment intensity and timing ref [8]. In parallel, the distinction between top-down and bottom-up connectivity provides a useful framework for separating patients dominated by goal-directed attentional control failure from those with impaired stimulus-driven reorienting, a distinction that could inform target selection and stimulation protocols ref [12].

Precision rehabilitation should also account for the heterogeneity of disturbed spatial operations. Neglect can reflect impaired spatial remapping across eye movements, suggesting that some patients may benefit less from generic attentional training and more from interventions explicitly targeting updating across gaze shifts ref [24]. This is especially relevant given the tight coupling between attention and pre-saccadic orienting, where deficits in anticipatory shifts of attention may constrain visual exploration, cancellation performance, and the functional gains achievable with therapy ref [26]. Incorporating oculomotor phenotyping into trials may therefore improve both response prediction and outcome sensitivity.

A further implication is that multimodal profiling should not be limited to visual-attentional measures alone. The proposal that neglect can include a vestibular component highlights the need to identify patients whose spatial bias is amplified by altered graviceptive or body-centered reference frames ref [14]. Such patients may require combined approaches that integrate non-invasive brain stimulation with sensory recalibration or vestibular-oriented rehabilitation rather than single-modality treatment. Overall, future trials should test biomarker-guided treatment allocation in which structural disconnection, connectivity signatures, oculomotor remapping deficits, and vestibular features are jointly used to personalize intervention pathways ref [8], ref [12], ref [14], ref [24], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central translational priority is biomarker-guided stratification. Neglect is not a unitary syndrome, and future trials should classify patients by structural disconnection, attentional state, and sensory-interactive deficits rather than by bedside diagnosis alone. Tractographic evidence that white-matter injury patterns relate to neglect expression supports the use of lesion-network markers to predict who is most likely to benefit from network-targeted stimulation or compensatory training ref [8]. This approach is also consistent with broader clinical descriptions emphasizing the marked heterogeneity of spatial disorders and their partially dissociable mechanisms ref [33].

Precision rehabilitation should also incorporate state-dependent physiological markers. Alertness strongly modulates both spatial and nonspatial attention, implying that fluctuations in arousal may partly determine whether a patient can engage with or respond to therapy ref [16]. In parallel, vestibular contributions to spatial cognition suggest that some patients may benefit from multimodal interventions that combine visuospatial training with vestibular or body-orientation manipulations, particularly when imbalance in egocentric reference frames is clinically prominent ref [26]. Together, these observations argue for adaptive protocols in which treatment intensity and modality are adjusted to a patient’s momentary cognitive state and dominant mechanistic deficit.

For non-invasive brain stimulation, the next step is to move beyond generic stimulation recipes toward mechanism-sensitive dosing. Work on TMS-induced perceptual effects underscores that stimulation outcomes depend on timing, cortical state, and the functional role of the targeted area, all of which should inform individualized protocols ref [27]. Likewise, the limited effect of high-gamma tACS over visual cortex on spatial attention, despite measurable perceptual benefits, cautions against assuming that any oscillatory intervention will generalize to neglect-relevant attentional functions ref [31]. Future translational studies should therefore pair stimulation with behavioral and imaging biomarkers to verify target engagement before large-scale efficacy testing.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central translational priority is to move from syndrome-level treatment toward mechanism-based stratification. Spatial neglect is not a unitary deficit: acute neglect and extinction can reflect dissociable functional states within the visuospatial attention system, implying that patients grouped under the same bedside label may require different therapeutic targets and stimulation parameters ref [15]. This heterogeneity is compounded by lesion-topography and network-level variability, as emphasized by neuroanatomical mapping work showing that parietal, frontal, and subcortical contributions cannot be reduced to a single cortical locus ref [19]. Precision neurorehabilitation therefore requires phenotyping that combines behavioral decomposition with lesion and network characterization before treatment allocation.

One practical implication is the incorporation of physiological and imaging biomarkers into trial enrichment and treatment monitoring. Perfusion-sensitive MRI has shown that neglect after basal ganglia stroke may be better explained by distributed cortical dysfunction than by focal structural injury alone, supporting the use of functional imaging to identify viable but dysregulated networks that could be modulated by non-invasive brain stimulation or targeted training ref [16]. Such biomarkers may help distinguish patients with potentially reversible diaschisis-like states from those with more fixed disconnection, and could be used to adapt dose, site, and timing of intervention over the course of recovery ref [19].

A second priority is to anchor efficacy to meaningful clinical outcomes. Neglect severity alone is insufficient: anosognosia, extinction, and lesion site all contribute to disability in activities of daily living after right-hemisphere stroke ref [15]. Future studies should therefore test multimodal, adaptive rehabilitation pathways in which biomarker-informed stimulation is paired with therapies addressing awareness, sustained engagement, and everyday functional transfer. This would better align mechanistic precision with real-world benefit while also clarifying which patient profiles are most likely to achieve durable gains ref [15], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A further translational priority is to move from static lesion-based treatment assignment toward state-sensitive neurorehabilitation. Work on anticipatory states and perceptual expectation shows that visual performance is strongly shaped by moment-to-moment preparatory dynamics, including under distractor conditions, suggesting that neglect severity may fluctuate with covert changes in temporal readiness and predictive set rather than only with fixed structural damage ref [7], ref [10], ref [23]. For rehabilitation, this implies that stimulation and behavioral training should be timed and titrated to the patient’s current attentional state, with online physiological monitoring used to identify periods of maximal receptivity.

Oscillatory markers are especially promising for this purpose. Alpha-band activity appears to carry perceptual expectations and modulate early visual responses, while trial-by-trial changes in instantaneous frequency predict alpha amplitude during perception ref [10], ref [11]. More broadly, attentional selection depends on large-scale oscillatory synchrony, providing a mechanistic bridge between local cortical excitability and distributed network coordination ref [30]. In neglect, these findings motivate biomarker-guided protocols in which EEG-derived indices of alpha power, frequency, or interregional coupling are used to personalize non-invasive brain stimulation parameters and to define mechanistic trial endpoints rather than relying solely on behavioral averages.

Finally, precision rehabilitation should also incorporate higher-order spatial priors. The concept of internal models for visual perception suggests that recovery may depend on restoring predictive mappings between body, eye, and world coordinates ref [23], while evidence on global orientation and hemispheric lateralization underscores that spatial cognition is embedded in broad reference-frame systems rather than isolated hemifield representations ref [25]. Future trials should therefore combine stimulation with tasks that recalibrate predictive spatial models across visual, postural, and exploratory domains, and should test whether changes in electrophysiological state markers mediate durable functional gains.
